newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Britain warns on public pay, deficit soars.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Britain warns on public pay, deficit soars.

text.p: The British government on Tuesday called for a public sector pay freeze as new figures showed that public finances deteriorated sharply in August.

Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke said next year's pay award to public sector workers should be lower than last year's four percent to help balance the books and reflect the lower rate of inflation.

"The government remains determined to contain public spending and suggests that pay recommendations for 1997 should be set at lower levels than this year to reflect the changed economic context," he said in his annual submission of evidence to the Pay Review Bodies.
"With inflation low and expected to continue to fall, public sector settlements must adjust to reflect this, and be affordable within budgets."
The government has been squeezing the public wage bill for several years in an effort to reduce overall public spending and make room for vote-winning tax cuts.

But official figures released on Tuesday showed spending outpaced tax revenue in August, forcing the government to borrow 4.5 billion pounds in the month compared with a surplus of 1.66 billion in July.

The Office for National Statistics said the Public Sector Borrowing Requirement (PSBR) stood at 13.37 billion pounds ($20.8 billion) in the first five months of the fiscal year compared with 16.72 billion in the same period last year.

The government shrugged off the news. A Treasury spokesman said the figures published in recent months were consistent with the government hitting its latest borrowing forecast of 27 billion pounds in the fiscal year.

But the figures were higher than expected and City analysts said the slump in indirect tax (VAT) receipts will make it more tricky for Clarke to cut taxes in the November budget, the last before a general election must be called by next May.
"Despite this we expect Clarke to cut taxes by around three billion pounds this November, which will be justified with offsetting public spending cuts," said Andrew Cates, UK economist at UBS.
He said the announcement on public pay was a further step in the direction of tighter public spending which is exceeding expectations.
"It looks like departmental spending is overshooting but in an election year its pretty hard to rein them back."
Public finances are the only major black spot in the economic recovery, which boasts steady output growth, rising consumer spending, low inflation and a housing market revival.

Britain's leading business lobby, the Confederation of British Industry (CBI), last month singled out the PSBR for criticism, saying it was much higher than it should be at this stage in the recovery.
But keeping a tight lid on public sector pay could backfire politically if the government is seen scrimping on cherished areas of expenditure like health and education to fund tax cuts.
Public sector union leaders immediately attacked the Chancellor's warning on pay.
"It's an indication the government does not really believe in high quality education," said Doug McAvoy, general secretary of the National Union of Teachers, the largest teaching union.
"Our teachers deserve better treatment. They have a right to expect that their salaries will reflect the importance of their work."
The ruling Conservatives are trailing opposition Labour by more than 20 points in the opinion polls, but the Conservatives are catching up.
Labour's lead has slipped from nearer 30 percent and all sides are predicting a bitter and protracted election campaign. ($1=.6428 Pound)
